content.text:
1. Our opening guess is settled: the mean of two numbers sits halfway between them, and for any data the distances on the two sides of the mean add up to the same total.
2. A value above the mean pulls the mean up, a value below pulls it down, and the median moves only when the middle moves.
3. Line graphs follow change over time. Still open for you: pick one graph from this chapter and write two questions it raises.

concepts.concept_name: Game of Hex

content.text: Game of Hex. Hex is a two-player strategy game played on a rhombus-shaped board made of hexagonal cells, usually of size 11 × 11. Each player is assigned a colour and two opposite sides of the board. Players take turns placing a piece of their colour on any empty cell. Once placed, pieces can not be moved or removed. The objective is to create an unbroken chain of one's own pieces connecting the two assigned sides. The first player to complete such a connection wins the game.

Each player is assigned a colour and two opposite sides of the board. Players take turns placing a piece of their colour on any empty cell. Once placed, pieces can not be moved or removed. The objective is to create an unbroken chain of one's own pieces connecting the two assigned sides. The first player to complete such a connection wins the game.

content.text:
1. Predict first: can a game of Hex end in a draw? Play a few rounds before you decide.
2. Each player must join their two sides with an unbroken chain, and blocking the other player also builds your own chain.
3. Play with a partner on paper and talk about the moves that helped.

content.text:
Worked example: On a 3 by 3 Hex board the players fill all 9 cells. Can the game end with neither player joining their two sides?
1. Try filling a small board in every way you can: one colour always joins its two sides.
2. A wall of one colour that blocks the other side is itself a chain across the board.
3. So a full board always has exactly one winner.
Answer: No; a Hex game can never end in a draw

objectives.objective_text: Students compute the mean family size from a frequency table by adding every value as many times as it occurs, and explain why averaging the distinct values is wrong.
Students locate the middle positions in a frequency table by adding frequencies, and name the median without writing out every value.
Students enter frequencies, see the total, the mean and the running totals update, and locate the median position for tables of their own.
Attempt each practice question independently, working through every step before viewing the video solution and checking the answer.

objectives.objective_text: Students locate a value from a column letter and a row number and describe a row or a column as a range written Start:End.
Students type a SUM or AVERAGE formula over a range to find a student's total or a subject's class average, and compare two subjects.
Students type an AVERAGE formula over a range of three cells to find Gowri's average marks and check it against adding the marks and dividing by three.
Students click cells, type SUM and AVERAGE formulae over rows and columns of the marks table, and check totals, subject averages and which of two subjects has the higher average.
Students compare a clustered column graph and a line graph of the same monthly temperatures and explain why a line graph suits data across time.
Students read a line graph in two steps, naming the axes, the scale and the marks first, then writing summary statements about the trend of each line.
Students enter or drag points from a table onto a labelled grid, join them in order, pick a scale that fits the values, and describe the shape of each line.
Attempt each practice question independently, working through every step before viewing the video solution and checking the answer.
objectives.strand_name: Visualising and Interpreting Data

objectives.objective_text: Students identify the given axes, scale and series on a graph of objects launched into space, and write valid summary statements, noting what is not shown.
Students compare changes between years by the steepness of line segments, judge whether given statements are valid inferences, and find two consecutive years where the count doubled.
Students count how many bars a clustered column graph of the same data would need and explain why the line graph is clearer for changes over time.
Students read values at marked points on several line graphs, compare steepness, test statements as valid or not valid, and write one summary statement for each graph.
Attempt each practice question independently, working through every step before viewing the video solution and checking the answer.

Students mark the six cities on a map, find each city's peak and low months, and relate rainfall timing to the west and the east coast.
Students place cities on a map of India, switch their rainfall lines on and off, mark peak and low months, and group the cities by when they get their rain.

objectives.objective_text: Students read the colour scale that maps the difference between rice and wheat eating from minus 100 to plus 100, and explain what a value of plus 100 means.
Students list the five states most preferring rice and wheat, name some balanced states, and estimate the hidden value for Karnataka from the values of its neighbours.
Students tap states to read their values, rank the top five on each side, drag a threshold to find balanced states, and place a guess for a hidden state before it is revealed.
Students match colours to activities with the key, work out the time of an activity from the box count, and infer which day of the week a strip shows and when a long movie happened.
Students sketch how their own weekday strip and a holiday strip would look, and compare them with an adult's strip, naming what is similar and different.
Students read a smooth line graph of sleep time over age, say why 80 points look like a curve, and compare the full graph with the zoomed one.
Students colour the 48 boxes of a strip with a key, read off the hours spent on each activity, and compare two strips box by box.
Students choose a question about their own day, decide what to record and for how many days, and describe how they will summarise and show the data.
Students choose one group investigation, either a week of family sleep or the daily timings of Grade 8 schools, and decide how to combine the data of all members using the mean and median.
Students enter their own day's data, see the mean, the median and a strip or graph update, compare with an adult or a group, and write findings and new questions.
Attempt each practice question independently, working through every step before viewing the video solution and checking the answer.
